content:
I remember at some point, maybe Lean v4.19 or so, coercions were pretty-printed with an up arrow ↑. However, testing it now, it seems like Coe.coe is used no matter what values I give to pp.coercions and pp.coercions.types. For example.

When was the pretty printed changed? Why? Is there a way to change it back?
It seems like it might be an issue of my setup, I tried using a project in v4.19.0 and it doesn't seem to be displayed any differently
attribute [coe] Coe.coe
Actually, it seems to be working fine with Int and Nat, so I guess there's something else going on
Coe.coe should (almost) never be used in the first place
Is there a reason for this? I was actually just in the middle of a conversation about this
Writing [Coe V E] is pretty much always a bad idea, you should probably only use it when you're defining your own Coe instance.

Yes, this is a minified example. I was thinking of embedding the instance into another one, as a requirement. Not sure if that improves the situation, but V and E are further related than just [Coe V E]
For a less minified example, it refers to this draft
attribute [coe] ToVal.coe.coe (or something along those lines)

Fernando LEAL said:

Is there a reason for this?

Yes — the way Coe works during elaboration is that the Coe gets unfolded after it's synthesized, putting the actual definition in place. If you use Coe directly, then this mechanism doesn't get activated.

The way arrow pretty printing works is that the functions that Coe unfolds to are manually tagged with @[coe].

Sometimes I wonder if the elaborator ought to unfold manual Coe.coe too, to help normalize expressions, but it's unclear if there are examples where this is required, or if it can be avoided.
In the case atop this thread it can't be unfolded anyway though, right?

Yeah, that's a case that won't be unfolded, since the instance is a free variable. I think things work out if [Coe ...] is only used as arguments to Coe instances, but locally, in the instance definition itself, you will see raw Coe.coe terms.

Kyle Miller said:

Fernando LEAL said:
If you use Coe directly, then this mechanism doesn't get activated.

But in the examples I linked above I don't use Coe.coe directly. It's just printed this way when displayed in the InfoView
You're using Coe directly by having it in a variable. There's nothing that this [Coe V E] instance can unfold to, since the instance is a free variable.

Ok, I understand then that what gets pretty printed to ↑ is not Coe.coe, but actually the concrete implementation of Coe.coe for the type being coerced, which is why when declaring my instance through a variable there is no such concrete implementation to map it to
When I was asking about whether using Coe.coe was ill-advised or not, I thought we were talking about how recommended or not it was to use coercions in general.

Yeah, to clarify, the recommendation is strictly about avoiding [Coe V E] arguments except in instance definitions, since otherwise you'll get raw Coe.coe expressions in your results, which might negatively affect theorem proving. I'm sure there are exceptions, but it's a reasonable first approximation.

Yeah, that makes sense. I think I can work around this in my usecase by defining a concrete coercion function for my typeclass, to which I give the [coe] attribute, and then just defining an instance which uses it.

In terms of my MWE, the solution I'm imagining is something like this
Yeah, that's a good design pattern, defining your own coercion class and hooking it into Coe. Mathlib uses it in at least a few places.
Great, thanks for the input! Always good to know I'm doing something sensible
